items.support: A measurable map T:X→X preserves μ when μ(T^-1 E)=μ(E) for every measurable E. A system is (X,A,μ,T). A probability system has μ(X)=1.
items.proof_plan: Use inverse images throughout; no assumption of invertibility or completeness.

items.support: An invertible system has a bijective T with measurable inverse. Invertibility modulo null sets means this holds on an invariant conull measurable restriction.
items.proof_plan: Distinguish actual bijection from invertibility modulo null sets and from measure preservation.

references.title: E–W §2.1 p.13; local sigma-finite uniqueness theorem

items.support: Let T be measurable and P generate A as a pi-system. Suppose P has increasing P_n covering X with μ(P_n)<∞ and μ(T^-1 P)=μ(P) for P in P. Then T preserves μ.
items.proof_plan: Define ν(E)=μ(T^-1 E); inverse images preserve disjoint unions, so ν is a measure. Apply the exact published uniqueness theorem. For finite measures add X to P.

references.title: E–W §2.1, Exercise 2.1.3; Sarig Proposition 1.4 completion argument

items.support: Compositions and nonnegative iterates of measure-preserving maps preserve measure. A Borel measure-preserving self-map extends as a measurable preserving map for the completed sigma-algebra.
items.proof_plan: Pull back identities; for completion sandwich a completed measurable set between a Borel set and a Borel null set, whose preimage is null.

items.support: For measurable f≥0, ∫f∘T=∫f in [0,∞]; for integrable real or complex f the same identity holds and f∘T is integrable. Conversely indicator integral invariance implies measure preservation.
items.proof_plan: Indicators, finite nonnegative simple functions, monotone convergence, then positive/negative and real/imaginary parts.

items.support: For 1≤p≤∞ set U_T[f]=[f∘T].
items.proof_plan: Pullbacks of null measurable sets are null; therefore the expression is independent of representatives.

items.support: For 1≤p≤∞, U_T is a well-defined linear isometry. It is onto for an invertible system.
items.proof_plan: For finite p use ∫|f∘T|^p=∫|f|^p; at infinity compare all superlevel null sets in both directions. Inverse composition provides surjectivity when applicable.
Both families contain only measurable sets. Do not assert they always differ: identity makes them equal.

items.support: I and I′ are sigma-algebras and I⊆I′.
items.proof_plan: Complement commutes with pullback; symmetric difference for a countable union is contained in the union of component symmetric differences.

references.title: E–W Proposition 2.14 pp.23–24; Sarig Proposition 1.1 pp.5–6

items.support: For E∈I′ the set F=limsup_n T^-n E lies in I and μ(E Δ F)=0.
items.proof_plan: Each E Δ T^-n E is null by telescoping; the countable union contains E Δ F. Dropping the first term of a limsup proves exact invariance. No completeness needed.

items.support: T is ergodic for μ if each E∈I has μ(E)=0 or μ(X\E)=0. On a probability space this means measure zero or one.
items.proof_plan: Name the measure. Permit general measures in the definition, but state subsequent probability hypotheses explicitly.

items.support: On a probability space ergodicity is equivalent to null/conull mod-null invariant sets, to every invariant measurable real or complex function being constant a.e., and to every f with f∘T=f a.e. being constant a.e.
items.proof_plan: For a.e. invariant f use rational level sets, countable unions and separation of two distinct real values. For exact invariant functions use indicator of a strict invariant set; the bridge supplies equivalence.

items.support: In an ergodic probability system, E of positive measure has μ(union_{n≥1}T^-n E)=1. Equivalently every pair A,B of positive measure has μ(B∩T^-n A)>0 for some n≥1.
items.proof_plan: The union pulls back into itself with equal finite measure, so is mod-null invariant. Use countable subadditivity and the complement of an invariant set for the converses.

items.support: Strong mixing means μ(A∩T^-n B)→μ(A)μ(B) for every A,B. Weak mixing means N^-1 sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|μ(A∩T^-n B)-μ(A)μ(B)|→0.
items.proof_plan: Absolute values occur inside the Cesaro sum. These definitions use probability normalization.

items.support: Every strongly mixing probability system is weakly mixing; every weakly mixing probability system is ergodic.
items.proof_plan: Split Cesaro averages into a finite initial segment and small tail; apply weak mixing to a strict invariant set against itself.

items.support: If μ(X)<∞ and an algebra C generates A, every E∈A can be approximated in μ(E Δ C) by C∈C.
items.proof_plan: The approximable sets form a sigma-algebra: complements preserve error and a countable union is first truncated using finite measure, then each of its finitely many terms is approximated.

references.title: E–W Exercise 2.7.3 pp.52–53 (pi-system extension by finite Boolean algebra)

items.support: For a measure-preserving probability system, correlations on a generating pi-system containing X suffice to check strong or weak mixing.
items.proof_plan: Extend to its finite Boolean algebra by finite inclusion-exclusion, then approximate both sets. The error is bounded uniformly in n by twice the sum of their symmetric-difference errors.

items.support: Strong or weak mixing is equivalently tested on complex L2 correlations, using conjugation in the second factor.
items.proof_plan: Approximate by bounded simple functions obtained by truncation and quantization; Cauchy–Schwarz makes the approximation error uniform in n. Indicator functions prove the reverse.

items.support: If μ(X)<∞ and W=E\ union_{n≥1}T^-n E, then T^-n W, n≥0, are pairwise disjoint and μ(W)=0.
items.proof_plan: If x belongs to preimages at i<j, T^i x∈W returns to E at time j-i, contradiction. N equal masses are bounded by μ(X).

items.support: For μ(X)<∞ and E measurable, almost every x∈E returns to E infinitely often at positive integer times.
items.proof_plan: Every finite-return point eventually enters W at its last visit; hence the exceptional set is contained in union_{n≥0}T^-n W. This also includes points with no positive return.

items.support: Let X have a countable open base contained in A and T preserve a finite measure. Outside a measurable null set, every neighborhood of x is revisited infinitely often. In a metric space there are n_j→∞ with T^{n_j}x→x.
items.proof_plan: Apply recurrence separately to every basis set, take the countable union of exceptional sets, and then choose the least succeeding time into a shrinking ball.

items.support: Assume μ(X)<∞. For E measurable of positive measure define r_E(x)=min{n≥1:T^n x∈E}, min empty=∞. On E∞=E∩limsup T^-n E put T_E(x)=T^{r_E(x)}x and μ_E=μ|E∞/μ(E).
items.proof_plan: Use the infinitely-returning core, not merely the first-return domain: it is conull in E and is mapped into itself.

items.support: r_E is measurable on E and T_E is measurable on E∞ with its trace sigma-algebra.
items.proof_plan: The level r_E=n is E∩T^-n E∩intersection_{1≤j<n}T^-j(E^c). On each level T_E=T^n; take countable unions of preimages.

items.support: For a finite measure-preserving system and μ(E)>0, T_E preserves μ|E∞ and μ_E; invertibility and ergodicity are not required.
items.proof_plan: For B⊆E∞ expand μ(B) by pulling back and splitting at E for N steps. The sum of first-return contributions is ≤μ(B). Apply the same inequality to E∞\B and use T_E^-1 E∞=E∞ to obtain equality.

items.support: If T is ergodic on a probability space and μ(E)>0, then T_E is ergodic for μ_E.
items.proof_plan: Extend a bounded T_E-invariant function along first entrance into E∞; sweep-out makes this defined a.e.; the extension is T-invariant, hence constant.

items.support: For an ergodic probability-preserving T and μ(E)>0, ∫_E r_E dμ=1; equivalently ∫r_E dμ_E=1/μ(E).
items.proof_plan: Let C_N=intersection_{j=0}^{N-1}T^-j(E^c). Pullback invariance gives μ(E∩{r_E>j})=μ(C_j)-μ(C_{j+1}), with C_0=X. Sum j<N, use sweep-out for μ(C_N)→0, then monotone convergence of tail sums.

items.support: In the same ergodic probability setting, ∫f dμ=∫_E sum_{j=0}^{r_E-1}f(T^j x)dμ for nonnegative measurable f and for integrable real/complex f.
items.proof_plan: Repeatedly split the integral into E and E^c after pullback. For bounded nonnegative f the remainder is ≤||f||∞ times the measure of avoiding E for N steps. Truncate and use monotone convergence; apply first to |f| before signed decomposition.

items.support: Use [0,1) with d(x,y)=min(|x-y|,1-|x-y|), Borel or completed Lebesgue measure λ, Rα(x)={x+α}, and D(x)={2x}.
items.proof_plan: Check the circle metric and countable arc base; distinguish it from the ordinary interval topology. Both maps are continuous in the circle metric.

items.support: Rα is an invertible λ-preserving circle map for every real α.
items.proof_plan: Split a wrapping interval at the endpoint, use translation invariance and the finite pi-system criterion, then completion.

references.title: E–W Proposition 2.16 p.26 and Example 2.33 p.49

items.support: If α is irrational then {nα mod 1:n∈Z} is dense. There are arbitrarily large positive n with d(nα,0) arbitrarily small.
items.proof_plan: Pigeonhole two of 0,α,...,Nα into the same one of N arcs. The nonzero difference is arbitrarily close to an integer; multiples give a fine net. Unboundedness follows because no fixed nonzero multiple is an integer.

items.support: Assume countable choice. Rα on the Lebesgue circle is ergodic iff α is irrational.
items.proof_plan: Rational case: finite union of short translates. Irrational case: take density points of an invariant set and its complement; choose a common small radius with both density ratios >0.9, and rotate the first center within radius/10 of the second using orbit density. The translated almost-full interval must overlap the other almost-full interval in positive measure, contradiction.

items.support: D is a non-injective λ-preserving map on the circle.
items.proof_plan: The preimage of [a,b) is [a/2,b/2) disjoint union [(a+1)/2,(b+1)/2); use the generator criterion and completion.

references.title: Sarig Proposition 1.5 p.9, conclusion; density argument is the MT-22 prescribed local replacement

items.support: Assume countable choice. D is ergodic for λ.
items.proof_plan: For a strict invariant A and every generation-n dyadic interval I, branch D^n maps I linearly onto [0,1), giving λ(A∩I)=λ(A)λ(I). A density point of A has dyadic density tending to one: I is contained in a centered interval of twice its length. Hence λ(A)=1 if positive.

items.support: Doubling is strongly mixing for λ.
items.proof_plan: For dyadic intervals of depths r,s and n≥r, direct branch counting gives λ(I∩D^-n J)=λ(I)λ(J). Apply the generator criterion.

items.support: On Ω={0,1}^{N_0}, prescribe finitely many coordinates; give a cylinder fixing k coordinates mass 2^-k, and finite disjoint unions the sum.
items.proof_plan: Use the algebra of finite unions of cylinders, not the collection of cylinders alone. Common refinement proves the content is well-defined and finitely additive.

references.title: E–W Examples 2.8–2.9 compact metric footnote; elementary binary-tree proof

items.support: The metric d(x,y)=2^-min{j:x_j≠y_j}, d(x,x)=0, has the cylinder topology and is compact in ZF.
items.proof_plan: If an open cover has no finite subcover, choose recursively the first binary child cylinder still having no finite subcover. The resulting unique path belongs to a covering open set which contains one of its prefix cylinders, contradiction. No arbitrary choice.

items.support: The fair-coin finitely additive content on the cylinder algebra is a premeasure.
items.proof_plan: A countable disjoint union in the algebra covering an algebra member is an open cover of a compact clopen set. A finite subcover reduces countable additivity to finite additivity; remaining members are empty.

references.title: E–W Examples 2.8–2.9 with local Caratheodory route

items.support: Assuming countable choice, there is a unique Borel probability on Ω with cylinder masses 2^-k. Its completion is also available.
items.proof_plan: Apply Caratheodory to the premeasure; prefix cylinders are a countable base, so the generated sigma-algebra is Borel. This is not a general infinite-product theorem.

items.support: The left shift σ(x)_j=x_{j+1} preserves fair-coin measure and is strongly mixing, hence ergodic.
items.proof_plan: Preimages preserve cylinder masses; widely separated coordinate sets give exactly independent cylinders by finite counting. Apply the generator criterion and mixing implication.

references.title: E–W §4.1 pp.97–98, replacing weak-star compactness with the design-required local argument

items.support: Assume countable choice. For nonempty compact metric K, C(K,R) has a countable uniformly dense family.
items.proof_plan: Choose countable dense {x_j}; distance functions d(·,x_j) separate points. Rational polynomials in finitely many of these and 1 form a countable family. Its real algebra is dense by Stone–Weierstrass; approximate the finite coefficient lists rationally.

references.title: E–W §4.1 pp.97–98; local diagonal/RMK replacement for source weak-star compactness

items.support: Assume countable choice. Every sequence of Borel probabilities on nonempty compact metric K has a subsequence whose integrals converge for every continuous real f to the integrals of a Borel probability.
items.proof_plan: Diagonalize bounded integrals on the countable dense family. Uniform estimates extend convergence to all C(K). The limit functional is positive, linear and sends 1 to 1. RMK represents it; compactness makes C_c=C.

items.support: Assume countable choice. Every continuous self-map T of a nonempty compact metric space K admits an invariant Borel probability.
items.proof_plan: Average point masses along one orbit and use the previous subsequence lemma. Telescoping bounds the discrepancy for f∘T and f by 2||f||∞/N. The pushforward is Borel and regular; RMK uniqueness gives equality. Do not invoke Banach–Alaoglu.

items.support: False even on a probability space.
items.proof_plan: D(0)=D(1/2), so actual invertibility fails. For mod-null invertibility both halves have overlapping image after removal of a null set by scaling; no conull restriction is injective.

items.support: False for an irrational circle rotation.
items.proof_plan: Return subsequence n_j α→0 gives correlation of a half-circle with itself tending to 1/2 instead of 1/4.

references.title: Katok–Thouvenot, §5.2.3, pp.696–697, Theorem 5.12 (prerequisite proof source; local supplier still absent)

items.support: Translation x↦x+1 on (R,λ) preserves measure but points of [0,1) never return.
items.proof_plan: Preimages translate sets, whereas positive iterates of [0,1) are disjoint from it.

items.support: An ergodic system can have nonempty proper strict invariant null sets.
items.proof_plan: For doubling the dyadic rationals in [0,1) form a nonempty proper null set with D^-1 Q_2=Q_2.

items.support: Doubling is λ-ergodic but the orbit of zero is {0}.
items.proof_plan: Zero is fixed and the circle has other points.

references.title: E–W ergodicity definition and doubling example; explicit measure specialization

items.support: A probability-preserving map may have only constant continuous invariant functions and yet fail measure ergodicity.
items.proof_plan: For D, f∘D=f and the density of preimages of zero force every continuous invariant f constant. Use μ=(δ_0+(δ_{1/3}+δ_{2/3})/2)/2; the invariant set of eventual preimages of 0 has μ=1/2.

items.support: For α=p/q in lowest terms, union_{j=0}^{q-1}[j/q,j/q+1/(2q)) is invariant and has measure 1/2.
items.proof_plan: Rotation permutes these intervals.
Compute both branches. Forward image D[0,1/2)=[0,1) has twice the measure.

items.support: The cylinders [0],[01],[101] have masses 1/2,1/4,1/8; [01] intersect σ^-3[10] has mass 1/16.
items.proof_plan: Count distinct prescribed coordinates; no probabilistic independence theorem is assumed.

items.support: Almost every x in [0,1/4) returns infinitely often to that interval under doubling.
items.proof_plan: Apply recurrence on the unit-probability circle. No every-point conclusion or return frequency is asserted.

items.support: For irrational α and E=[0,1/2], ∫_E r_E dλ=1 and the normalized mean is 2.
items.proof_plan: Apply Kac with λ(E)=1/2. Endpoints change no integral; no assertion that each return time equals two.

items.support: E={0} is mod-null invariant under D but D^-1 E={0,1/2} differs from E.
items.proof_plan: Both finite sets are null; calculate the preimage.

references.title: E–W Definition 2.13 and periodic orbit specialization

items.support: D is ergodic for λ and δ_0, but not for μ=(δ_0+(δ_{1/3}+δ_{2/3})/2)/2.
items.proof_plan: The two periodic-orbit probabilities are invariant; their mixture assigns mass 1/2 to the strict invariant eventual-zero set. This corrects the design’s false δ_0 counterexample.

items.support: An irrational rotation is not weakly mixing for λ.
items.proof_plan: Use f(x)=exp(2πix), whose mean is zero and whose absolute self-correlation at every iterate is one. This is one explicit function computation, not the Fourier-series ergodicity proof.

items.support: For identity on [0,1] and E=[0,1/2], r_E=1 but ∫_E r_E dλ=1/2.
items.proof_plan: Compute directly; normalized mean is one, not 1/λ(E).

items.support: On [0,1), define G(0)=0 and G(x)={1/x}. The probability with density 1/(log(2)(1+x)) is invariant.
items.proof_plan: Use inverse branches x=1/(n+y): transformed densities telescope as sum_{n≥1}1/((n+y)(n+y+1))=1/(1+y). Handle branch endpoints as a countable null set. Ergodicity is deferred, not used.
